newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair promises "tough love" in Europe.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair promises "tough love" in Europe.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair is promising a constructive new approach to Europe at Friday's informal meeting of European leaders, ending years of confrontation under the Conservatives.
But behind the warmer tone lies a steely determination not to give ground on key issues like border controls, which could once again leave Britain at odds with its European partners.

Aides said Blair would offer "dialogue not war, solutions not confrontations" when he meets his European Union colleagues in the Dutch seaside town of Noordwijk for a special summit for them to get to know Britain's new leader.
But continued British control of its borders was "sacrosanct", they said.
With continental European states arguing that border controls should be brought under the control of the EU, the stage is set for tough talking.
One of Blair's closest aides was keen to dismiss suggestions that Britain would once again be on its own against the rest.
"I don't think it's necessary to go into this first foray into Europe talking about vetos," he said.
Yet Blair has just three weeks beofre an Amsterdam summit to help shape crucial reforms designed to prepare the EU for the entry of former East Bloc states and the challenges of the next century.
Aides said Blair would make clear he believes his huge parliamentary majority of 179 seats will allow Britain once again to become a major player in Europe after years of "impotence and defeatism".

He is expected to tell other European leaders that the European "elites" have lost touch with their citizens and that unease about the pace of integration is not confined to Britain, which opposes any moves towards a European superstate.
One of the first to feel the steel rather than the warmth is likely to be European Commission President Jacques Santer.
Blair was angered by a Santer speech during Britain's election campaign criticising those opposed to closer European integration.
The speech was seen as potentially damaging to Labour in the crucial days before the May 1 poll, and sources made clear that the "elites" included Santer.

But Blair will also be seeking to correct a perceived slight in talks with Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi after Foreign Secretary Robin Cook angered Italy by saying Britain wanted to take its place in Europe alongside France and Germany.
"It was in no way intended as a snub, far from it," said an aide.
Blair will also be looking for a pay-off for his government's warmer tone.

The Labour government has already agreed to end Major's opt-out for Britain from the social chapter on worker rights and has promised to fall into line with its European partners on measures aimed at bosting employment, environmental protection and consumer protection.
"What is in his mind is a determination to get a better deal for Britain from Europe," the senior aide said.
